genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure answers calls from people in distress
early in her career she raised the volume of her voice
that approach pushed callers to break off the exchange
she completely overhauled her way of speaking
she now leaves pauses and slows her delivery
she repeats the last word the caller has said
the caller's breathing eventually falls in with hers
her colleagues have taken up the same method
she says this work has changed how she hears the people around her
text: The woman on the helpline takes calls from people in trouble, and she keeps her voice low on purpose. Early on she did the opposite: she pushed her voice up to cover the panic at the other end. It backfired. Callers stiffened, cut her off, hung up before she got anywhere. So she turned the whole thing around. Now she leaves silences, she slows down, she takes the last word a caller says and hands it back. Little by little the breathing on the line falls in with hers, and the tightness on the line eases without either of them naming it. She shrugs when she explains this, as if it were plain. Her colleagues copied her once they saw their own calls holding longer. One thing still makes her smile: the work taught her to hear the people at home, and she had thought she knew them already.

units: the piece passes judgment on an exhibition devoted to the emotions
the first part of the route piles up video installations
that accumulation wears out the attention of visitors
the emotions are presented there in a distant and didactic way
the second part offers a space with no screen at all
there you listen to accounts of grief spoken by strangers
the public slows down there and shows feeling
the final stage invites you to set down on paper the emotion hardest to name
the reviewer advises walking the place in the opposite direction
text: You come out of this exhibition about the emotions with mixed feelings. The trouble starts with the layout. Screen after screen, room after room, the video installations pile up, and the visitor, worn out well before the halfway mark, ends up skimming past every one of them. Anger, shame and joy get the same cool, explanatory treatment, so nothing ever stirs. The people who built it seem to have worked that out, because the second half pulls the show back. One bare room, no screen anywhere, asks you to listen while strangers describe a grief. The quiet in that room does the work on its own, and the crowd slows down, lingers, doubles back. The last stage goes further still: you write on a slip the emotion you find hardest to name. Worth the trip, then, provided you begin at the end and walk it backward.

units: the addressee has asked a question about the kinship between two feelings
the writer describes fear as a pressure applied to the back of the neck
fear dampens the palms and shortens the breath
grief is compared to a wet weight that covers you
fear pushes you to move whereas grief holds you still
both feelings slip away when you try to look at them head on
both settle when you put them into words in front of someone
the writer explains in this way why he writes so often
the writer says he prefers an awkward sentence to a piece of advice
text: Your question has stayed with me since your letter came: is grief anything like fear? I turned it over by the window, and here is what I think. Fear is a hand laid on the back of your neck. It grips, it presses, it wants you up and moving. It leaves your palms damp and your breath short. Grief presses nothing. It settles. It lies over your chest like a soaked blanket and asks you to stop. One speeds you up, the other slows you down, and that is the clearest line between them. On one point, though, they are twins, and that point has occupied me all winter. Both slip away the moment you look straight at them, and both loosen their hold once you say them out loud to somebody. That is why I write to you so often. Write back. Your clumsiest sentence steadies me better than advice.

units: specialists draw a line between an emotion and a mood
three criteria underpin that distinction
an emotion is brief whereas a mood stretches out further
an emotion relates to a target you can pick out
a mood has no addressee you can assign to it
the third criterion concerns the traces you can observe in the body
you cannot shut down the firing of an emotion by will
you can on the other hand shape how it shows
fear sends blood toward the muscles to make the body ready to act
text: Is an emotion the same thing as a mood? The question comes up again and again. Specialists say no, and they set out three criteria. The first is duration: an emotion flares and dies away fast, while a mood stretches over a far wider span. The second is the object. An emotion aims at something you can point to, whereas a mood drifts with nothing to land on and nobody to fasten itself to. The third is the mark left in the body, which shows up in heart rate, sweating and muscle tension. Can an emotion be shut down by willpower? The answer has to be qualified. You can shape how it shows, you cannot cancel the moment it fires. And what is fear good for? It gets the body ready to act by pushing blood toward the muscles, which is why your hands clench and your throat goes tight without your ever deciding on it.

units: the practitioner opens the session with a harmless question about meals
the young boy claims he cannot remember
the young boy closes up and folds his arms
the practitioner switches subject and mentions the sound of the rain
the young boy admits that he dreads family meals
he explains that the people at the table stare at him
the practitioner asks him which seat he would rather take
he points out the far end of the table, next to the door
the practitioner suggests he raise the subject at home
he ends up agreeing and announces that he will come back
text: The session opened on a question that seemed to lead nowhere: the psychologist asked the boy what he had eaten the evening before. He said he could not remember, then went quiet and folded his arms tight across his chest. She let it go without pressing him and talked instead about the rain hitting the window and the color the sky had taken. After a while he said that family meals frightened him, because everyone around the table watched him the whole time, from the first dish to the last. She asked where he would sit if the choice were his. He said he would take the far end of the table, right beside the door. She suggested he bring it up at home, in his own words. He hesitated, and then he agreed. On his way out he said he would be back, and he smiled without turning around.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: healers of long ago put the states of the soul down to inner fluids
that theory appealed because it offered a remedy people could carry out
low spirits were treated through diet or through the drawing of blood
one failure after another weakened the belief
direct observation took over from the theory
some healers noted identical signs for fear and for rage
they tied those states to the nerves rather than to a fluid
suffering of the mind stopped being seen as a stain to be driven out
out of that reversal came the idea that speech given a hearing can heal
text: Long before anyone thought to measure, healers explained the states of the soul by inner fluids that had to be brought back into balance. The theory held because it handed people something to do: if low spirits came from an excess, then a change of diet or an opened vein ought to drain it off. One failure after another wore the belief thin, and looking closely took over from reasoning. Physicians noticed that fear and rage left the same marks on patients who had nothing else in common, and they concluded that such states belonged to the nerves and not to any liquid. The consequence ran deep. Suffering of the mind stopped being handled as a stain to be flushed out, and people began to question it instead. Out of that turn grew the idea that speech, carefully heard, could heal.

units: speaking in front of an audience speeds up the heart and dampens the hands
the voice turns shaky in that situation
fear itself is not to blame since it makes the body ready to act
the trouble comes from the thoughts added on top of the fear
you picture the humiliation ahead and watch for unfriendly faces
that watching drives the alarm higher still
the first countermove is to make the out-breath longer than the in-breath
that lengthening settles the pace of the heart
the second countermove is to put your attention on a receptive listener
moving attention outward breaks the vicious circle
text: You know the feeling. You stand up to speak in front of a room, your heart starts pounding, your palms turn cold and damp, and your voice comes out with a wobble in it. Fear is not the culprit here, since fear gets the body ready to move. What sinks you is everything you stack on top of it. You picture yourself making a fool of yourself, you scan the room for a hard face, and the alarm inside you climbs another notch. Two small moves get you out. Breathe out longer than you breathe in, because a long exhale pulls the heartbeat down. Then look after somebody other than yourself: find the most attentive face in the room and speak to that person. Turn your attention outward and the loop has nothing left to feed on. Your hands may still shake a little. You will get to the end anyway.

units: two men have been waiting for the same medical test since the same hour
the first reads a magazine and mentions his vegetable patch
the second checks the display board over and over
the second half rises each time a name is called out
both men say they feel the same worry
the first tells himself he will soon be given some information
the second expects the worst outcome
a nurse predicts that the second will walk out wrung dry
the nurse reckons that a word can turn the experience of waiting around
text: Two men have been sitting in the same waiting room since the same hour, booked in for the very same test. One leafs through a magazine with his shoulders loose and says he is thinking about his vegetable patch. The other keeps checking the board above the door, and he half rises every time a name carries down the corridor. Ask them and both will tell you they feel the same dread. The difference sits somewhere else entirely. One is telling himself he will soon know where he stands, the other is telling himself he will soon hear the worst. A nurse who has watched this play out for years says the second man will walk out wrung dry, while the first will walk out merely relieved. She adds that a single sentence, dropped at the right moment, can tip a wait from one side to the other.

units: get hold of a thin notebook and keep it on you for a week
each evening you write three lines and no more
the first line names the dominant feeling with a precise term
you set aside vague terms in favor of exact words
the second line gives the place in the body where the feeling showed up
the third line names the event that came before the feeling
you forbid yourself any rereading before the week is out
rereading too soon bends what you noticed
at the end you spread the pages out to spot what keeps returning
the exercise is run again in the following season
text: Pick up a thin notebook, the kind that slides into a back pocket, and keep it on you for a whole week. In the evening, open it on your knees and write three lines, no more than that. On the first, name the feeling that took over, using the sharpest word you can reach for: not bad, but tightness, or heaviness, or lift. On the second, write where in the body it settled, whether the throat, the neck or the stomach. On the third, name whatever came just before it, even if the link looks thin to you. Read nothing back until the week is out, because rereading too soon bends what you saw. On the last evening, spread the pages in front of you and look for what keeps returning. You will find repeats that memory alone would never have held. Close the notebook without judging it, and run the whole thing again next season.

units: a research team ran a protocol in two similar hospital wards
the first stage consisted of measuring without stepping in
the measures covered the pulse and the sweating of the nursing staff
peaks were recorded at the moment of the spoken handovers between teams
the second stage imposed a short break before every handover
the instruction asked for the breathing to be slowed during that break
the third stage set the readings of the two wards against each other
the ward given the break showed better pulse variability
the authors stay cautious because the load on each team differs
text: A research team started its protocol at the beginning of the cold season, in two hospital wards chosen for how closely they matched. The first stage recorded heart rate and sweating in the nursing staff across their shifts, with nobody stepping in to change anything. When the readings came back, the spikes clustered around one moment: the spoken handover between teams. The second stage put a short, compulsory pause before every handover, with instructions to slow the breathing while it lasted. The third stage set the figures from the two wards side by side. The gap widened week after week, and the ward with the pause showed steadier heart rate variability along with fewer damp hands. The authors stop short of claiming much, since the two teams do not carry the same load.
